newsitem.title: USA: Illinois misses deadline on power deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Illinois misses deadline on power deregulation.

text.p: A bid to deregulate the Illinois electricity market was dealt a setback after state legislators, electric utilities and consumer groups failed this week to agree how to move ahead, lawmakers said.

The 70-member group failed Monday to meet a self-imposed deadline to hammer out a master deregulation plan, prompting lawmakers to warn they now face drafting legislation without the backing of key interested parties.
Because of the controversial and far-reaching nature of dismantling traditional utility monopolies, this could make eventual passage of a bill more difficult.

The meetings, which were held over the past two months and chaired by the Illinois Retail Merchants Assoc, failed to find consensus on issues like stranded costs, rate reductions, and a timetable for when the market will be open to competition.
Illinois state representative Vincent Persico, R-Glen Ellyn, speaking to reporters on Monday, said legislators are now going to have to make crucial decisions on open issues.

If there isn't movement toward a bill within the next couple of weeks, Persico said it might take up to two years before all the various groups affected could reach agreement on a master deregulation plan.

The spring legislative session ends in two weeks, and though there was speculation a new effort might be made to bridge differences between the various parties, no further meetings of the 70-member group have been scheduled.

Low-cost power producers like Peoria-based Central Illinois Light Co (Cilco), a unit of CILCORP Inc, backed by out-of-state power marketers like Enron Corp, are pushing for immediate retail competition and minimal stranded cost recovery.
At the other end of the spectrum are companies like Chicago-based giant Commonwealth Edison, a subsidiary of Unicom Corp, and Decatur-based Illinois Power Co, a unit of Illinova Corp.

Both utilities have huge stranded costs, mostly in the form of nuclear power plants built during the days of a strictly regulated market, and are pushing for full recovery of these costs, estimated at around $5 billion for ComEd.
Illinois Power and ComEd favor a gradual deregulation plan that would phase in open competion over five to seven years and use power transmission fees to cover stranded costs.
Governor Jim Edgar, citing the high cost of power in Illinois compared with neighboring states, has made deregulation a priority of his administration.
Edgar has estimated competition among power suppliers could save Illinois consumers 30 percent on their electricity bills.
